In brief

Episode 4 re-starts the novel in two ways, both prompted by Homer's Odyssey. It introduces a new protagonist, Leopold Bloom, whose opening chapters (4-6) offer numerous precise parallels to Stephen's (1-3). This structure recalls Homer's introduction of Telemachus (books 1-4) and Odysseus (5-8). Homer's opening in medias res is followed by a long flashback as Odysseus tells the Phaeacians the story of his many adventures after the fall of Troy (9-12). Ulysses features no corresponding flashback but chapters 4-15 are preceded by a Roman numeral II, signifying that they echo Odysseus's long struggle to get from Troy to Ithaca. Although Stephen figures importantly in four of these episodes, the primary focus is on Bloom. Chapter 4 finds him at home on Eccles Street and nearby Dorset Street on the northern edge of central Dublin. The schemas call this chapter "Calypso," suggesting that it corresponds to book 5 of the Odyssey, where the hero is seen unhappily enslaved by a beautiful nymph who keeps him from going home. Since Bloom is at home with his wife Molly, readers are encouraged to wonder whether all is well in the marriage.

At more length

Among the many parallels between Stephen's first three chapters and Bloom's are the temporal frames in which the action takes place: approximately 8-8:45 AM for both Telemachus and Calypso, approximately 9:30-10:30 for Nestor and Lotus Eaters, and approximately 11 AM-noon for Proteus and Hades. Homer is not so precise about Telemachus's efforts to discover news about his father and Odysseus's journey from Calypso's island to that of the Phaeacians, but both are presented as happening in present time, relative to the flashback, and readers may imagine them to be roughly synchronous. The impression of actions happening on parallel tracks will be recapitulated later when Odysseus and Telemachus converge on the swineherd's hut on their way to the palace in Ithaca.

Odysseus is first seen on an island called Ogygia, where, desperately unhappy, he longs to return to Ithaca. He has been away from home for twenty years, seven of them in the company of a demi-goddess who gives him her love, her body, and a promise of immortality, but not the freedom to return home. Bloom's story begins at home, for the necessary reason that this is where he begins every day, but the Homeric symbolism implies that he is an unhappy exile. So, as Bloom contentedly begins an ordinary day—bringing meat to his house, preparing breakfast, collecting the mail, discussing things with his wife, tending to the needs of his cat, clearing his bowels and his bladder—readers may wonder why Joyce wanted to suggest that his home is a place of desperate dissatisfaction.

Athena tells Zeus that her protégé "lives and grieves upon that island / in thralldom to the nymph." When the messenger god Hermes arrives at Calypso's cave, bearing Zeus' command to release her prisoner, Odysseus is not present. He is on the seashore, sitting "apart, as a thousand times before":

The sweet days of his lifetime
were running out in anguish over his exile,
for long ago the nymph had ceased to please.
Though he fought shy of her and her desire,
he lay with her each night, for she compelled him.
But when day came he sat on the rocky shore
and broke his own heart groaning, with eyes wet
scanning the bare horizon of the sea.
(5.150-57, trans. Fitzgerald)

Joyce's Calypso reproduces much of this domestic arrangement. Molly plays the role of the captor, ordering her husband about with sharp commands, and he dutifully labors to fulfill her needs and indulge her whims. She is also the sexual partner who has "ceased to please," and here too Joyce supplies a realistic analogue to Homer's story, though he takes many chapters to supply the details. Since the death of their second child, more than ten years earlier, the Blooms have not enjoyed satisfying sexual intercourse, and the disinterest is pretty clearly Bloom's.

Many other details link Molly with Calypso. Homer calls his goddess "the softly-braided nymph," and Molly lies in bed "counting the strands of her hair, smiling, braiding." Over the Blooms' bed hangs a reproduction of a painting titled The Bath of the Nymph, which Bloom thinks is "Not unlike her with her hair down: slimmer." He remembers how it came to hang there: "She said it would look nice over the bed." A passage in the Odyssey describing the scented smoke in Calypso's cave seems to have inspired Bloom's appreciation for the scents of tea and cooking food in Molly's presence. And the name Calypso means "Concealer." When Bloom delivers a letter to his wife, she hides it under the pillow. It is from the man that she will begin an affair with later in the day.

Molly does not bother to effectively hide either the letter or the affair from her husband, but her brazenness expresses alienation from him better than any furtive precautions could. Bloom too feels alienated. He spends much of his day thinking about other women, beginning in this chapter with the neighbors' servant girl. Although he is not conducting any physical affairs, he has visited prostitutes, and June 16 finds him engaged in an epistolary affair. It is probably not his first. His marked subservience to Molly coheres with a tendency to masochism, a deferential manner suggestive of poor self-confidence, a willingness to imagine other men having sex with his wife, and an interest in Greek goddesses as immortal ideals of physical beauty who do not have to live with physical frailty.

Bloom likes his place in the world, his home with Molly. The "art" of the fourth chapter, according to Gilbert's schema, is "economics," which in its original Greek sense means household management, and this term describes Bloom's life as a househusband puttering about in Calypso. But the letter under the pillow announces that his nest is about to be invaded, and as he makes his way about Dublin on June 16 he cannot stop thinking about the impending tryst. Joyce may possibly have intended Boylan's letter as a symbolic analogue of Hermes' message from Zeus, telling Odysseus that it is time to leave. Bloom takes a very long time to come back to Eccles Street, avoiding his house like the plague. Between his 9 AM departure and his return in the wee hours of the morning he undergoes a series of adventures that Joyce analogizes, one by one, to those in the Odyssey.

In book 23 Odysseus and Penelope lie in bed catching up on the last twenty years, and he tells her of his adventures in chronological order. Joyce freely altered this order of events. The following list shows the books in which Homer narrates them, and then their corresponding chapters in Ulysses:

Cicones            9      (absent)
Lotus-Eaters        9       5
Cyclops            9      12
Aeolus             10      7
Laestrygonia         10      8
Circe            10      15
Hades            11      6
Sirens            12      11
Wandering Rocks      12      10   
Scylla and Charybdis   12      9
Oxen of the Sun      12      14
Ogygia (Calypso)      5      4
Phaeacia (Nausicaa)     6       13

Ogygia and Phaeacia come at the end of the chronology, but in Homer's narrative they come first, as the immediate precursors to Odysseus's return to Ithaca. After Odysseus tells the Phaeacians of his many trials, fully half of the poem remains: returning to Ithaca (13), meeting the loyal Eumaeus (14), reuniting with Telemachus (15-16), returning to the palace and slaughtering the suitors (17-22), reuniting with Penelope (23), dealing with a potentially violent aftermath (24). Joyce reduces this climactic action to just three chapters: the union of Bloom and Stephen in Eumaeus (16), the return to the patriarchal domain in Ithaca (17), and what Molly thinks about it all in Penelope (18).

John Hunt 2025
